## Early draft — not reviewed, please treat with caution
This page was put together quickly with AI assistance. We have *not* checked it carefully
ourselves, and we have *not* run it past Pablo or any field experts. Numbers, framings,
and the little calculator below could all be wrong or misleading; treat everything here as
a first pass meant to start a conversation, not a finding.

It discusses external work by Pablo Antonio Moreno Casares (Pablo AMC) and builds a
deliberately simplified bridge from our cost model to his demand model. His
[interactive model](https://pabloamc.github.io/Cultivated_meat/interactive.html) is the
authoritative source for the demand side — our bridge only approximates a slice of it.
Corrections very welcome via [Hypothesis](https://hypothes.is/) (the `<` tab at right)
or the [discussion hub](https://github.com/unjournal/cm_pq_modeling/discussions/3).
:::

**Return to:** [Interactive Cost Model](index.qmd) | [TEA Comparison](compare.qmd) | [Learn](learn.qmd) | [Limits/Critique](limits.qmd)

## The two models are complementary halves of one pipeline

In July 2026 Pablo AMC published *["Cultivating hope: calibrating the expectations for
cultivated meat to end factory farming"](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/ED2ag8hYTWf4kmL3x/cultivating-hope-calibrating-the-expectations-for-cultivated)*,
with an accompanying [interactive economic model](https://pabloamc.github.io/Cultivated_meat/interactive.html).
It has two parts: (1) a review of the same TEA literature we model, and (2) a
**demand-side** model that takes a cost per kg as given and asks *what market share
would consumers choose at that price?*

Our model and his answer different questions and connect end-to-end:

```{=html}
<div style="margin:14px 0; padding:12px 14px; border:1px solid #d4dfd4; border-radius:8px; background:#f8f9f5; font-size:14px;">
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse;">
<tr>
  <td style="vertical-align:top; width:47%; padding:6px 10px;">
    <strong>Our model (supply / cost)</strong><br>
    Bottom-up Monte Carlo TEA. Media, micronutrients, growth factors, capital and
    operating costs → a distribution of cost per kg for a target year (default 2036).
  </td>
  <td style="vertical-align:middle; width:6%; text-align:center; font-size:15px; color:#2d4a2d; white-space:nowrap;">$/kg&nbsp;→</td>
  <td style="vertical-align:top; width:47%; padding:6px 10px;">
    <strong>Pablo's model (demand / adoption)</strong><br>
    Takes cost as <em>exogenous</em>. Cost → retail price ratio → discrete-choice
    (logit) market share by species, product tier, and geography → diffusion over time.
  </td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>
```

Because he pins price from the same TEAs we build bottom-up (Humbird 2021, Pasitka 2024,
Negulescu 2023, CE Delft, GFI), our cost distribution is a natural input to his demand
model. Neither of us models the other's half: we do not model demand or adoption; he does
not model supply, economies of scale, or how the market would clear.

## Where the two agree, differ, and what's new

On agreements: we draw on the same source literature and read it the same way. Humbird's
2021 pessimism was driven mostly by amino-acid/media cost, which is not a hard
thermodynamic constraint and which Pasitka's 2024 empirical work (hydrolysate at
$0.63/L) pushed down sharply. Both of us conclude cultivated meat likely lands a few-fold
above conventional meat — not at parity, but not orders of magnitude off either.

Differences that matter:

- *Scope.* We are supply-side and end at a cost distribution; he is demand-side and ends
  at market shares. His is the piece we have explicitly not built.
- *Cost level and spread.* His headline biomass figure is $15–30/kg (point read ~$25/kg).
  Our default is higher and much wider — median ~$56/kg, 5–95% roughly $15–310/kg. It is
  tempting to attribute this to our adding capital and operating costs, but that is a
  small part of it:
  <span title="From 300k Monte Carlo draws of our default model: median CAPEX + fixed OPEX ≈ $6.7/kg, about 12% of the $56 median. Media alone is the median ~$35/kg; total variable cost median ~$48/kg.">in our model capital + fixed operating cost is only ~12% of the median (~$7/kg)</span>.
  The real driver is media: our *median* media cost is ~$35/kg, versus the ~$14/kg
  biomass media Pasitka reports and Pablo adopts. So even stripping our CAPEX/OPEX
  entirely, our variable-cost median (~$48/kg) sits well above his ~$25. The gap is
  mostly that our priors on media intensity (litres of medium per kg) and medium price
  are wider and centred higher than his single empirical point — plus a fat right tail
  that pulls our *mean* ($97/kg) far above our median. He instead reads the optimistic
  end of the same literature.
- *Treatment of uncertainty.* Ours is fundamentally a distribution (30k+ Monte Carlo
  draws over structural priors); his exposes uncertainty through user-tuned sliders and
  a lighter Monte Carlo band on the demand parameters.
- *What drives the answer.* For us it is media intensity, growth-factor cost, reactor
  capital, and financing. For him it is the price ratio R plus behavioural terms — loss
  aversion, a "real meat" credit, authenticity/provenance penalties, and food neophobia —
  none of which appear anywhere in a cost TEA.

Genuinely new in his work, relative to ours:

- *Species inversion.* The cheap, feed-efficient meats (chicken, pork) are the hardest to
  displace because conventional price is already low; expensive meats (beef, seafood) and
  luxury goods are the most penetrable. This is a demand result our cost model cannot
  produce.
- *Beachhead logic.* Foie gras as the standout entry product — luxury price, unstructured
  (little scaffolding), and already ethically stigmatized or banned in places. Also
  high-end fish, tuna, salmon.
- *Disruption framing.* An innovation-economics argument (Christensen's
  <span title="From Clayton Christensen's 'The Innovator's Dilemma': new technologies rarely win by beating incumbents on the mainstream buyer's existing priorities. They take root in an underserved niche the incumbent ignores, improve, then move upmarket — the path Pablo argues cultivated meat must follow, as electric cars did.">disruptive-innovation theory</span>)
  that improving on incumbents' own dimensions usually fails; cultivated meat needs an
  underserved segment (vegan/vegetarian attrition, "vegan veto" restaurants,
  biosecurity-sensitive buyers) plus government or advocacy push, much as electric cars did.
- *Behavioural realism.* A random-utility model with an explicit "real meat vs.
  from-an-animal" separation (GFI's thesis), neophobia that decays with exposure, and
  income-elasticity effects (would AGI-driven abundance change adoption? — modestly).

## How credible is each, and where are they weak?

Neither is authoritative; both are explicitly AI-assisted, work-in-progress framings.

Our cost model — strengths: first-principles structure, honest wide uncertainty, a
latent "maturity" factor tying technology adoption to financing, and a documented
external critique with responses ([Limits/Critique](limits.qmd)). Weaknesses: an ad hoc
dependence structure, supplemental proteins (albumin, transferrin, insulin) handled
coarsely, sensitivity presented as a dollar-swing ranking rather than a variance
decomposition, and a fat right tail that some readers find implausibly pessimistic.

Pablo's demand model — strengths: it fills the half we skip; it is calibrated to real
data moments (plant-based ~1.2% share and its 89% mainstream split, Gallup veg+vegan ~5%,
meat elasticities), it validates out-of-sample against plant-based *milk*, and the
species-inversion and beachhead conclusions are robust to the diffusion form (which only
sets speed, not the ceiling). Weaknesses he flags himself: (a) price elasticities are
measured on today's marginal choices but applied to a not-yet-existing product at very
different maturity; (b) the
<span title="Bass diffusion model: a classic marketing S-curve for how a new product spreads, splitting adopters into 'innovators' who try it independently and 'imitators' pulled in by word-of-mouth. It was designed for one-time purchases of durable goods (TVs, cars), so applying it to repeat grocery buying is a stretch — Pablo uses it only to set how fast adoption approaches its ceiling, not the ceiling itself.">Bass diffusion S-curve</span>
is built for first-purchase durables, not repeat grocery buys; (c) several behavioural
weights are solved to hit calibration targets rather than independently measured;
(d) the scaffold cost ($6/kg) is an unsourced assumption; (e) precision fermentation
(egg, dairy) is out of scope for want of a good TEA.

Which is more credible? They are not rivals — they are not estimating the same quantity.
On the shared cost question, Pablo reads the optimistic end of a range our distribution
also covers; our median is higher mostly because of our wider, higher media-cost priors
and fat tail, not (as one might assume) because of capital and operating costs. His demand
results are the more novel and, within their stated caveats, the more decision-relevant
contribution: even a cheap cultivated product may capture little chicken or pork share,
which reframes what "success" looks like.

## Interactive bridge: from a cost per kg to a market share

The calculator below takes a cultivated biomass cost (seed it with our model's output, or
with Pablo's optimistic read) and runs a much-simplified version of his cost-to-share
logic: delivered cost → retail
<span title="Price ratio R = cultivated delivered cost ÷ conventional retail price. R = 1 means price parity; R = 2 means cultivated costs twice as much as the conventional product it competes with.">price ratio R</span>
against each species' conventional US price → a two-way conventional-vs-cultivated
<span title="Logit / discrete-choice share: a standard economics way to turn a 'how much better or worse is option A than option B' score into a probability that a consumer picks A. Larger score → larger share, following an S-shaped curve.">logit share</span>.

::: {.callout-important collapse="false"}
## This is NOT Pablo's model — it is a rough stand-in. Read before trusting any number.
Pablo's real model is a two-segment, four-product random-utility system with income
effects, loss aversion, and diffusion timing. What runs below is **none of that**. It is a
one-line approximation we wrote to build intuition: a single-attribute logit whose slope
we simply *reverse-engineered* to pass through two numbers Pablo reports — at price parity
(R = 1) about 49% share, and at R ≈ 2.4 about 9% share — and to which we then bolt the
per-tier authenticity offsets he documents (mince +0.2, cut −0.4, premium −1.5; foie gras
treated as unstructured and stigmatized, so a small penalty). It **omits** his two consumer
segments, the outside "whole-food" option, income effects, loss aversion, and all
diffusion timing. Because it is pinned to only two of his points, it can only reproduce the
*shape* of his story (cheap species resist, expensive and luxury ones are penetrable), not
his actual per-species shares. **For any number you would cite, use
[his interactive model](https://pabloamc.github.io/Cultivated_meat/interactive.html), not this.**
We would happily replace this with a faithful port, or with his own code, if he is open to it.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof cbio = Inputs.range([5, 120], {value: 56, step: 1, label: "Cultivated biomass cost ($/kg)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof markup = Inputs.range([0, 10], {value: 5, step: 0.5, label: "Retail markup m ($/kg)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof scaffold_cut = Inputs.range([0, 12], {value: 6, step: 0.5, label: "Scaffold cost for structured cuts k ($/kg)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const setC = (v) => {
    viewof cbio.value = v;
    viewof cbio.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
  };
  const btn = (label, v) => {
    const b = html`<button style="padding:5px 11px; font-size:12.5px; cursor:pointer; border:1px solid #2d4a2d; border-radius:6px; background:#2d4a2d; color:white;">${label}</button>`;
    b.onclick = () => setC(v);
    return b;
  };
  return html`<div style="margin:2px 0 12px; display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; gap:8px; align-items:center;">
    <span style="font-size:12.5px; color:#555;">Reference cost points — click to load:</span>
    ${btn("Our model median ($56)", 56)}
    ${btn("Our model p5 (optimistic, $15)", 15)}

    ${btn("Pasitka best future (~$22)", 22)}
  </div>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// --- Simplified port of Pablo AMC's Stage 1-2 (cost -> price ratio -> share) ---
// Calibration: logit slope gamma pinned to his two reported points:
//   share(R=1)   ~ 0.49  ->  logit ~  0.00 (constant c0)
//   share(R=2.4) ~ 0.09  ->  logit ~ -2.31 at ln(2.4)=0.875  ->  gamma = 2.64
gamma = 2.64
c0 = -0.04
logistic = (x) => 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-x))

// Species: approximate 2025 US retail price ($/kg) + tier + authenticity offset tau.
// Prices are rounded from US averages (per lb x 2.2046 = per kg):
//   Chicken breast boneless ~$4.17/lb -> ~$9/kg (BLS/FRED APU0000FF1101, late 2025)
//   Pork chops ~$4.1/lb -> ~$9/kg (BLS Average Price program)
//   Ground beef 100% ~$4.56/lb -> ~$10/kg (FRED APU0000703112, 2025)
//   Beef steak (avg of cuts) ~$10.2/lb -> ~$22/kg (BLS/USDA ERS, 2025)
//   Salmon fillet ~$11/lb -> ~$24/kg (typical US retail; no single BLS series)
//   Foie gras ~$80/kg -> illustrative luxury anchor only, NOT an official price series
// Tier "unstructured" => no scaffold cost; "cut" => scaffold applies.
species = [
  {name: "Chicken breast", pc: 9,  tier: "cut",          tau: -0.4, structured: true},
  {name: "Pork",           pc: 9,  tier: "cut",          tau: -0.4, structured: true},
  {name: "Ground beef",    pc: 10, tier: "mince",        tau: +0.2, structured: false},
  {name: "Beef steak",     pc: 22, tier: "cut (premium)",tau: -0.4, structured: true},
  {name: "Salmon",         pc: 24, tier: "cut",          tau: -0.4, structured: true},
  {name: "Foie gras",      pc: 80, tier: "luxury/unstructured", tau: +0.1, structured: false},
]

rows = species.map(s => {
  const delivered = cbio + (s.structured ? scaffold_cut : 0) + markup
  const R = delivered / s.pc
  const share = logistic(c0 - gamma * Math.log(R) + s.tau)
  return {name: s.name, tier: s.tier, pc: s.pc, delivered, R, share}
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div style="overflow-x:auto; max-width:100%;">
<table style="width:100%; min-width:620px; border-collapse:collapse; font-size:13.5px; margin:8px 0;">
<thead><tr style="background:#2c3e50; color:white;">
  <th style="padding:8px; text-align:left;">Species (tier)</th>
  <th style="padding:8px; text-align:right; white-space:nowrap;">Conv. price $/kg</th>
  <th style="padding:8px; text-align:right; white-space:nowrap;">Cultivated $/kg</th>
  <th style="padding:8px; text-align:right; white-space:nowrap;">Ratio R</th>
  <th style="padding:8px; text-align:left;">Estimated cultivated share</th>
</tr></thead>
<tbody>
${rows.map(r => html`<tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #dee2e6;">
  <td style="padding:7px 8px;">${r.name} <span style="color:#888; font-size:11.5px;">(${r.tier})</span></td>
  <td style="padding:7px 8px; text-align:right;">$${r.pc.toFixed(0)}</td>
  <td style="padding:7px 8px; text-align:right;">$${r.delivered.toFixed(0)}</td>
  <td style="padding:7px 8px; text-align:right;">${r.R.toFixed(2)}×</td>
  <td style="padding:7px 8px;">
    <div style="display:flex; align-items:center; gap:8px;">
      <div style="flex:0 0 46px; text-align:right; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;">${(r.share*100).toFixed(1)}%</div>
      <div style="flex:1; background:#eef1ee; border-radius:4px; height:12px; overflow:hidden;">
        <div style="width:${Math.min(100, r.share*100)}%; height:100%; background:${r.share>0.3?'#2d7a2d':r.share>0.08?'#c8862b':'#b04a4a'};"></div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </td>
</tr>`)}
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<p style="font-size:12px; color:#666; margin-top:6px;">
Share colour: green &gt; 30%, amber 8–30%, red &lt; 8%. Ordering across species is
driven almost entirely by the price ratio R (cost fixed, conventional price varies),
plus the per-tier authenticity offset — reproducing Pablo's inversion: cheap chicken and
pork resist, expensive beef, seafood, and luxury foie gras are penetrable.<br>
Conventional prices are rounded 2025 US retail averages (per lb × 2.2 = per kg): chicken
breast ~$9/kg and pork ~$9/kg (US BLS Average Price / FRED series), ground beef ~$10/kg
(FRED APU0000703112), steak ~$22/kg (BLS/USDA ERS). Salmon ~$24/kg is a typical retail
figure without a single official series; foie gras ~$80/kg is an illustrative luxury
anchor, not an official price. Change any of these and the ordering can shift.
</p>`
```

Try loading "Our model median ($56)" versus "Pablo optimistic (~$25)" and watch the shares
move. Even at the optimistic cost, chicken and pork stay near-zero while foie gras clears
easily — the demand-side result that a cheaper product does not by itself rescue the
feed-efficient species. At our more pessimistic median the whole picture shifts down, which
is why the cost half of the pipeline still matters.

## Possible next steps for reconciliation

- *Feed the full distribution, not a point.* Pipe our 30k-draw cost distribution into his
  cost-to-share step to produce a share distribution per species, rather than reading one
  cost point at a time.
- *Reconcile the media priors.* The $25-vs-$56 gap is mostly media cost, not capital or
  operating cost. The productive comparison is our priors on medium price ($/L) and media
  intensity (L/kg) against Pasitka's empirical point that Pablo adopts — where should the
  central estimate sit, and how wide should the tail be?
- *Joint parameters.* His scaffold ($6/kg) and markup ($5/kg) assumptions are exactly the
  kind of parameter our elicitation and workshop process could put priors on.
- *Conversation.* Pablo invited collaboration; the [CM workshop](https://uj-cm-workshop.netlify.app/)
  crux-mapping between "skeptics and optimists" is a natural venue.
